author: Dwarkesh Patel
title: Why I Don't Think AGI Is Right Around the Corner
central_scenario_summary: Current LLMs cannot learn continually on the job, which is why they cannot function as actual employees; if progress stopped today, less than a quarter of white-collar employment would be automated. Patel's central 50/50 timelines: computer-use agents that can do a week-long project (small-business taxes end-to-end) by 2028, and human-like organic on-the-job learning for any white-collar work by 2032. Once continual learning is solved, models that amalgamate learning across all copies produce a 'broadly deployed intelligence explosion' and functionally rapid superintelligence—so he is bearish on the next few years but expects a wild, transformative world within roughly a decade, with AGI probability per year cratering after 2030 if it hasn't happened.

capability_pace.notes: Central scenario is a drop-in white-collar worker within ~7 years (scale 3); he explicitly flags that this milestone shades into a broadly deployed intelligence explosion (scale 4) shortly after. Wide, lognormal distribution acknowledged.

expertise_erosion.notes: No position on entry barriers to expert occupations or expertise premia; the essay is about capability timelines, not skill distribution.

quotes.text: we might still see something that looks like a broadly deployed intelligence explosion. AIs will be getting broadly deployed through the economy, doing different jobs and learning while doing them
even if we stay sober about the current limitations of AI, we have to expect some truly crazy outcomes.

productivity_breadth.notes: Near term narrow ('If AI progress totally stalls today, I think <25% of white collar employment goes away'); central scenario by early 2030s is economy-wide and transformative. Scored on the central scenario.

quotes.text: So one AI is basically learning how to do every single job in the world.
their inability to build up context will make it impossible to have them operate as actual employees at your firm.
quotes.location: 'Continual learning' section (present-day limitation, removed in central scenario)

substitution.notes: Framing is explicitly about AIs replacing human employees once continual learning is solved; today's AI is a weak substitute only because of the learning bottleneck. No discussion of complementary task creation.

demand_absorption.notes: Silent on whether demand absorbs productivity gains or on new consumption categories.

mobility_adjustment.notes: Silent on worker reallocation, retraining, or labor-market institutions.

rent_concentration.notes: Silent on who captures the surplus; discusses labs' release incentives only in passing.

timeline_years.notes: 50/50 date of 2032 for the milestone he equates with 'at minimum a broadly deployed intelligence explosion', ~7 years from writing (June 2025). Computer-use milestone 2028.

inequality_prediction.notes: The essay makes no prediction about inequality or income distribution.
